title: Syntax you can see
summary: An introduction to reading X_eTaL, panel by panel after its syntax poster: an underline marks a function, a small letter above says where a name came from, a quote passes a function, small numbers pick an axis or a power, a box marks the system, a question mark guards, and square brackets make a train. Ends on the poster itself.

scenes.heading: Syntax you can see
scenes.narration: Code is {read|red} far more often than it is written. So this array language puts the meaning where your eye already is, in how each name looks. Here is how to {read|read} it, one idea at a time, from its syntax poster.
lines: Code is read more often than it is written.
So typography carries the meaning.

scenes.heading: 1. Function or value
scenes.narration: Start with the first letter. When it is underlined, the name is a function, like reverse. With no underline, the name is a value, a number, a list, or a table.
lines: Underlined first letter: a function.
No underline: a value.

scenes.heading: 1. Where a name came from
scenes.narration: A small letter above the name says where it came from. One mark for your own program, another for a name from a library, another for a helper that only this file can see. So you never hunt for a definition.
lines: Your program's own; a library's export;
a helper, this file only; a macro library's export.

scenes.heading: 2. Import a library
scenes.narration: Importing a library gives it a short name of your choosing. That name then shows above every word you use from it, so a reader knows which library to open.
lines: The alias you choose shows on every name it gives you.

scenes.heading: 3. Definitions
scenes.narration: The left arrow binds a name, to a value or to a function. But the equals sign never binds. It only compares, and gives ones and zeros.
lines: The arrow binds.
Equals only compares.

scenes.heading: 4. Apply or pass
scenes.narration: Write a function next to a value, and it applies to it. Put a quote in front of a function, and you pass the function itself, as a value, to another function. That is how each and reduce get their work.
lines: Next to a value: the function applies.
A quote in front: the function is passed.

scenes.heading: 5. Axes
scenes.narration: A small number below a function attaches an axis to it. Reduce sums down the first axis by default. With a two below it, it sums along the second axis instead.
lines: A number below: the axis it works along.

scenes.heading: 5. Rotate and transpose
scenes.narration: The same mark works for rotate and transpose. Rotate along axis two shifts every row. Transpose with no axis reverses them all, so rows become columns.
lines: Rotate along axis 2; transpose every axis.

scenes.heading: 6. Power
scenes.narration: A small number above a value is a power, so x squared looks the way it does on paper. Above a function, it applies the function that many times. Life to the fourth runs four generations, and the glider moves.
lines: Above a value: a power.
Above a function: apply it that many times.

scenes.heading: 7. Lambdas
scenes.narration: Braces make a function with no name. Alpha is its left argument, and omega its right. Or name the arguments with an arrow, and even take a pair apart.
lines: Alpha on the left, omega on the right.
Named arguments: a pair taken apart and swapped.

scenes.heading: 8. System names
scenes.narration: A box in front of a name marks the system, the things a program asks of the world outside. Reading and writing files, reading a typed line, drawing cells, or showing a picture.
lines: A box marks the system. It is still underlined: a function.

scenes.heading: 9. The question mark
scenes.narration: Between a test and a result, a question mark is a guard. When the number is at most one, the answer is one. The diamond separates statements. At the end of a name, the same mark is just part of the name.

lines.xtl: u:f_act := { n -> n <= 1 ? 1; n * u:f_act n - 1 }

lines: A guard: when the test holds, this result.
At the end of a name: part of the name.

scenes.heading: 10. Typed as ASCII
scenes.narration: You type all of this on an ordinary keyboard, with no special keys. An underscore after the first letter makes the underline, and a caret makes the small number above. The editor draws the rest.
lines: Typed on any keyboard, drawn like this:
An underscore after the first letter: the underline.
A caret: the small number above.

scenes.heading: 11. Trains
scenes.narration: Square brackets build a train, functions joined with no argument named. Two functions run one after the other. Three make a fork, so the sum divided by the count is the mean.
lines: Two: one after the other.
Three, a fork: sum over count, the mean.

scenes.heading: The syntax poster
scenes.narration: That is the whole poster, online, with every sample drawn by the language itself. Each train is checked against its spelled out form, so the poster cannot lie.

scenes.heading: Try it
scenes.narration: Try it in the playground in your browser, and keep the poster open beside it. The links are below.
